query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Reducing the degree of Cu segregation at grain boundaries in the FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy (HEA) coating will enhance its wear resistance and reduce deleterious microscopic deformation (grain boundary sliding and dislocation slipping) during high-temperature sliding.
generation.material_initial_state: A FeNiCrCoCu HEA coating exhibiting moderate phase separation with Cu-rich grain boundaries similar to the baseline condition.
generation.intervention: Processing modification (e.g., increased quenching rate or alternative thermal treatment) to minimize the extent of Cu segregation at grain boundaries compared to the baseline condition.
generation.conditions: Sliding contact tests conducted at the intended high-temperature operating regime (e.g., temperatures where diffusion and dislocation activity are significantly activated, such as >500°C) on a conventional metal substrate.
generation.structural_mediator: The concentration and distribution of Cu at grain boundaries acting as weak interfaces that facilitate premature grain boundary sliding and dislocation slipping.
generation.mechanism: High Cu concentration at grain boundaries lowers the critical resolved shear stress locally, promoting grain boundary sliding and uneven stress distribution during high-temperature sliding. Reducing Cu segregation leads to a more uniform grain boundary composition and improved mechanical cohesion, thereby mitigating deformation mechanisms that contribute to wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified HEA coating with reduced Cu enrichment at grain boundaries will exhibit lower wear rates and reduced microscopic deformation (less grain boundary sliding and dislocation activity) compared to the baseline coating under identical high-temperature sliding conditions.
generation.baseline: The current HEA coating condition with moderate phase separation and noticeable Cu-rich grain boundaries which have been associated with reduced ductility and strength in tension (as per molecular dynamics simulation evidence).
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to be valid under high-temperature sliding conditions where thermal activation promotes dislocation and grain boundary processes; deviations might occur at temperatures outside this regime or if other degradation phenomena (e.g., oxidation) dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The available evidence is based on molecular dynamics simulations of uniaxial tensile deformation and phase separation effects, not directly on sliding wear at high temperature. The translation of these mechanisms from tensile loading to sliding wear, and the impact of the substrate-coating interface, require further experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu HEA coatings on conventional metal substrates: one prepared under the baseline processing conditions (with typical Cu segregation) and another with modified processing designed to reduce Cu segregation at grain boundaries. Conduct high-temperature sliding wear tests under identical controlled conditions (e.g., fixed load, speed, and temperature above 500°C). Use surface profilometry, wear rate measurements, and microscopic evaluation (e.g., SEM and TEM analyses) to characterize wear tracks and deformation mechanisms.
measurements: Wear rate (mass loss and wear track dimensions)
Microstructural observations (grain boundaries, dislocation density, grain boundary sliding features)
Surface hardness and coating integrity before and after testing
High-temperature deformation characterization via in situ or ex situ microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the processed HEA coating with reduced Cu segregation does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and microscopic deformation (grain boundary sliding and dislocation activity) compared to the baseline coating under high-temperature sliding, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractPhase separation phenomena in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted much attention since their discovery, but little attention has been given to the dynamics of the deformation mechanism of this kind of HEA during uniaxial tension, which limits their widespread and practical utility. In this work, molecular dynamics simulation was used to study the effect of phase separation on the mechanical properties of an HEA under uniaxial tensile loading. Moreover, the associated deformation behavior of the Co–Cr–Cu–Fe–Ni HEA was investigated at the nanoscale. Models with Cu-rich grain boundaries or grains were constructed. The results showed that Cu-rich grain boundaries or grains lowered the strength of the Co–Cr–Cu–Fe–Ni HEA, and Cu-rich grain boundaries significantly reduced ductility. This change of mechanical properties was closely associated with a deformation behavior. Furthermore, the deformation behavior was affected by the critical resolved shear stress of Cu-rich and Cu-depleted regions and the uneven stress distribution caused by phase separation.
